headline: Flights near normal for Monday; oil steady after Bahrain attack; inflation report at 8:30
briefing: U.S. flight schedules should be close to normal on Monday, with about 144 cancellations listed so far against roughly 2,300 on Sunday, but check cross-border flights before heading to Pearson. Oil opened steady Sunday night, with Brent just under US$96 a barrel, despite Iran's claimed drone attack on a U.S. base in Bahrain. Canada's October inflation report arrives at 8:30 a.m. Monday, the same day about 18,000 north Etobicoke homes lose door-to-door mail.

keyDates.label: Canada inflation report; Etobicoke mail change
keyDates.why: Statistics Canada reports October consumer prices at 8:30 a.m., the last reading before the Bank of Canada's next decision; door-to-door mail ends for about 18,000 north Etobicoke homes; and U.S. aviation officials brief congressional staff on Friday's air traffic failure.

keyDates.label: Ukraine arms meeting; Nvidia results
keyDates.why: Ukraine's military backers meet at NATO headquarters in Brussels, Nvidia is due to report quarterly results amid its leadership crisis, and Israel's parliament is expected to vote on a new speaker.

keyDates.label: APEC summit; Alaska ranked-choice count
keyDates.why: Leaders meet in Shenzhen on Nov. 18–19, where Carney is to see Xi and the White House says Trump will meet Putin and Xi together; Alaska also tabulates its Peltola–Sullivan Senate race if no one tops 50%.

keyDates.label: Senate Democrats vote; Stelco recall
keyDates.why: Democratic senators choose between Chuck Schumer and Chris Van Hollen for majority leader by secret ballot, and 175 laid-off Stelco workers are due back in Hamilton.

keyDates.label: Bank of Canada and Fed rate decisions
keyDates.why: Both central banks decide the same day; Monday's Canadian inflation report will shape whether the Bank of Canada raises rates again.

keyDates.label: U.S. government funding deadline
keyDates.why: Federal funding runs out unless the outgoing Congress passes a spending bill or a temporary extension, which is also the likeliest vehicle for any new air traffic control money.

stories.headline: Duffy wants billions to replace contractor-run FAA network; Monday cancellations far lower
stories.summary: U.S. airlines cancelled about 2,300 flights on Sunday, the third day of disruption after Friday's nationwide ground stop, but only about 144 were cancelled for Monday as of Sunday afternoon. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy is asking Congress for tens of billions of dollars to replace the contractor-run network behind the failure, and Democrats say most of the money already approved is unspent.
stories.now: Flight tracker FlightAware counted 2,291 U.S. cancellations by 3 p.m. Eastern on Sunday, after 9,132 on Friday and more than 6,000 on Saturday; for Monday it showed 144 cancellations and 641 delays as of Sunday afternoon. Duffy said operations should be close to normal Sunday and fully normal Monday. He has traced the failure to a router at a Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) site in El Dorado, Arkansas, and said a second router in Texas also flooded the network with data; the routers' maker told the Wall Street Journal its devices worked as designed. Duffy said there are 69 routers of that type across the national airspace, that their ability to broadcast data has been switched off, and that there is no sign of a hack. On NBC's Meet the Press he said contractor L3Harris owns and runs the FAA's communications network under a decades-old contract, and The Hill reported he is seeking billions of dollars from Congress to replace it. President Donald Trump urged Congress to approve the money quickly and blamed the Biden administration. Democrats, who take control of Congress in January, point to US$12.5 billion approved in 2025 for air traffic modernization, of which Duffy says about one-third has been spent; Rep. Rosa DeLauro called the US$50-billion request a ransom, while Duffy says the existing money cannot legally be used for a new telecommunications network. FAA and Transportation Department officials are to brief congressional staff on Monday. In Canada, Air Canada cancelled about 250 flights on Friday, affecting roughly 27,000 passengers, and the Globe and Mail reported a further 63 on Saturday.
stories.backstory: A ground stop is an order that keeps aircraft from taking off; planes already in the air continue to their destinations. Nationwide stops are very rare: CTV reported that Friday's was only the second halt of all U.S. departures since the Sept. 11, 2001 attacks, the other being a January 2023 failure of a pilot-notification system. The FAA's telecommunications network has caused regional stoppages before, including one in the Minneapolis area in August. Canada's own air traffic system was not affected, and the Greater Toronto Airports Authority said Pearson's systems were working normally. The outage came a day after an unrelated Microsoft email failure, and officials have not linked the two.

timeline.event: Telecommunications problem halts Minneapolis-area flights for about 90 minutes

stories.why: A single network fault stopped departures across the world's busiest aviation system for hours, which raises questions about the age and resilience of U.S. air traffic control equipment. The administration is using it to press Congress for modernization money, and officials have warned similar failures could recur without upgrades.
stories.impact: If you are flying between the GTA and the U.S. on Monday, check your flight with the airline before leaving for Pearson or Billy Bishop; most schedules should be back to normal, but some aircraft and crews may still be out of position and rebooked seats are scarce. Under Canada's air passenger rules, airlines must rebook or refund you when a flight is cancelled, though cash compensation generally does not apply to disruptions outside the airline's control.

stories.headline: Oil opens steady after Iran's claimed drone attack on a U.S. base in Bahrain
stories.summary: Oil prices were little changed when trading resumed Sunday evening, with Brent crude just under US$96 a barrel, after Iran's Revolutionary Guards said they sent drones at a U.S. radar at a helicopter base in Bahrain. Bahrain says it shot the attacks down, and Iran's claims have not been independently verified.
stories.now: Bloomberg reported Sunday evening that Brent crude was holding just under US$96 a barrel and the U.S. benchmark, West Texas Intermediate, was near US$89, after Brent fell more than 2% last week. Traders are weighing the new attack against a finding last week by the International Energy Agency that world oil supply exceeded demand for the first time since the war began. Earlier Sunday, Iran's Revolutionary Guards said six of their drones targeted a U.S. air defence radar at the Al-Riffa helicopter base in Bahrain, calling it a response to a strike on a telecommunications tower in the Iranian port of Sirik. Bahrain's military said it intercepted and destroyed several Iranian aerial attacks before they reached their targets, issued its first nationwide safety alerts since September, and said it holds Iran fully responsible. Bloomberg described it as Iran's first strike on a Persian Gulf state in weeks, and no damage to the radar has been confirmed; U.S. Central Command rejected a similar Iranian claim on Friday, saying its forces shot down two attack drones with no injuries or damage. Iranian claims that tankers struck mines in and near the Strait of Hormuz on Saturday have still not been confirmed by any maritime authority. No new U.S. strikes on Iran have been reported, and people familiar with the matter say President Trump has told advisers he may hold off unless provoked.
stories.backstory: The U.S. and Israel began striking Iran on Feb. 28, and Iran choked traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, route for about a fifth of the world's oil. A June peace memorandum briefly reopened it but collapsed in July, and the U.S. imposed a blockade on Iranian shipping. Qatar gave Iran a new draft deal on Oct. 25. Trump has said the war will end soon, one way or the other.

timeline.event: Trump says no deal with Iran is needed; Brent settles at US$95.82

stories.why: Oil prices are the main driver of higher inflation in Canada and the U.S.; the October spike is why the Bank of Canada raised rates on Oct. 28.
stories.impact: Lower crude usually reaches GTA gas pumps within days, and this month's drop has eased fuel and delivery costs. Sunday night's calm opening suggests the Bahrain attack has not, so far, reversed that; a confirmed hit on U.S. forces or on tankers, or new U.S. strikes, could still push oil back up quickly.

stories.headline: Carney: U.S. trade deal is closer, but not without a viable auto sector
stories.summary: Speaking in Manila on Saturday, Prime Minister Mark Carney said talks with Washington are making progress and a two-country deal is possible, but that Canada is not there yet. He said he will not sign any agreement that fails to keep Canada's auto industry viable.
stories.now: Carney told reporters that keeping a viable Canadian auto sector is a condition Ottawa will not trade away, and described autos as one of the hardest issues in the negotiations. He said he recently had a substantive call with President Donald Trump that also included U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and White House chief of staff Stephen Miller. CBC noted the comments come about three months after Canada walked away from talks when Washington made late demands that included concessions on autos. Carney also said his government is not satisfied with what he called the partial approach Stellantis has taken in Canada, a reference to the sale of the Brampton plant. The Associated Press reported that Carney said Washington has dropped earlier demands touching Canada's cultural policies, French-language protections and its freedom to negotiate trade deals with other countries. No date for a deal or a next negotiating round was given, and Trump has threatened new tariffs on Canadian-made vehicles starting in January. Carney said a two-country deal with Washington is possible but that the sides are not there yet. Democrats who take control of Congress in January have said repealing tariffs on Canadian goods is an early priority, but they lack the two-thirds majorities needed to override a presidential veto.
stories.backstory: The United States has imposed tariffs on Canadian steel, aluminum, vehicles and other goods since 2025, and Canada answered with counter-tariffs plus relief programs for its own importers. Washington announced further tariffs on Canadian goods in July, and Canada pulled out of negotiations in the summer after last-minute U.S. demands. The North American trade pact known as CUSMA in Canada and USMCA in the United States is also under review. After Democrats won Congress on Nov. 3, Carney said the Trump administration is still the side Canada has to negotiate with.

timeline.event: U.S. announces new tariffs on Canadian goods

stories.why: A deal with Washington would do more for the Canadian economy than any new agreement in Asia, because about three-quarters of Canada's exports go to the United States. Carney's condition signals that Ottawa would rather wait than accept terms that shrink auto assembly in Canada.
stories.impact: Ontario's auto plants and parts suppliers, including those in Brampton, Oakville, Oshawa, Alliston and Windsor, depend on tariff-free access to the U.S. market, so the terms on autos matter directly for jobs in the GTA. Until a deal is signed, existing tariffs and counter-tariffs stay in place, which keeps some vehicle, steel and consumer prices higher.

stories.headline: Ottawa and Ontario still seeking Stellantis CEO meeting as Brampton plant sale clock runs
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney said Saturday that his government is not satisfied with Stellantis's approach in Canada, and tied the future of the auto sector to trade talks with Washington. Ottawa and Ontario are still waiting to put their package to stop the Brampton plant sale to global chief executive Antonio Filosa.
stories.now: Speaking in Manila on Saturday, Carney said the government is in no way satisfied with the current situation or with what he called Stellantis's partial approach to its Canadian operations, and said Canada will not sign a U.S. trade deal that leaves the auto sector unviable. Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said Friday that Ottawa is still trying to find a way to prevent the sale to armoured-vehicle maker Roshel, working with Ontario and with Unifor, the union for more than 9,000 Stellantis workers in Canada; she described the offer as an aggressive package but gave no details of what is in it. Ontario Economic Development Minister Vic Fedeli said the aim of meeting Filosa is to buy some time by getting the company to slow the sale down, and that the province has not advanced any money for Brampton so far; he said any support for the scenarios Unifor has proposed would come from Ontario's existing $2.5-billion auto support fund. No date for the Filosa meeting has been announced. Joly has said Ottawa cannot block the sale under the Investment Canada Act because the seller is a Canadian subsidiary, so its leverage is the subsidy agreement: up to $529 million was committed in 2022 for the Brampton and Windsor plants, and Stellantis has offered to return $24 million. The 30-day default period began Thursday, and Stellantis expects the sale to close by the end of the year.
stories.backstory: The Brampton plant built Dodge and Chrysler cars and has been idle for about three years while workers stayed on paid layoff. In May 2022 Ottawa agreed to give Stellantis $529 million to retool its Brampton and Windsor plants, and the company had planned to build the Jeep Compass in Brampton. In October 2025 it moved that vehicle to Illinois as U.S. tariffs on Canadian-made cars took hold. Stellantis signed a memorandum of understanding with Roshel in September, Unifor's contract expired Sept. 20, and the union declared an impasse over the plant's future.

timeline.event: Stellantis signs memorandum with Roshel; Unifor contract expires

stories.why: The sale ends hopes that a major GTA auto plant would restart vehicle production, and it tests whether governments can enforce the conditions attached to public subsidies. It also shows how U.S. tariffs are pulling auto investment out of Ontario.
stories.impact: Thousands of Peel Region families depend on the plant and its parts suppliers, and most laid-off workers have no guarantee of a job with the new owner. Taxpayers have a stake on both sides: any new support package would be public money, and the gap between the $24 million Stellantis has offered and what Ottawa says it is owed may end up in court.

stories.headline: Canada's October inflation report lands Monday at 8:30 a.m., with forecasts from 3.0% to 3.3%
stories.summary: Statistics Canada reports October consumer prices on Monday, the last inflation reading before the Bank of Canada's Dec. 9 rate decision. Economists expect the annual rate to stay close to September's 3.1%, but disagree on whether high energy costs are spreading to other prices.
stories.now: A Reuters poll of economists points to 3.2%, up from 3.1% in September. RBC expects a slight easing to 3.0%, with core inflation, which strips out volatile items, slipping to 1.9% from 2.1%; Continuum Economics forecasts 3.3%, which would be the highest since December 2023. Desjardins economist LJ Valencia expects a reading similar to or slightly above September's. CIBC's Avery Shenfeld and Helen Lao argue inflation will not climb as much as the Bank of Canada projects, which would leave less need for more rate increases. The central bank has said it expects inflation to stay above 3% through much of 2027, and one market report Friday put the odds of a December hike at about 64%.
stories.backstory: Oil prices jumped after the U.S.-Iran war disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz this year, and fuel costs have pushed up inflation since. Canada's annual rate rose to 3.1% in September, led by gasoline, while core measures stayed near 2%. On Oct. 28 the Bank of Canada raised its policy rate to 2.5%, its first increase in more than three years, and said more hikes were possible. Oil has since fallen from a late-October peak above US$117 to the mid-US$90s.

timeline.event: Inflation at 3.0%

Bank of Canada raises its rate to 2.5%
October inflation report due
Next Bank of Canada rate decision

stories.why: Monday's number is the main piece of evidence the Bank of Canada will have before deciding whether to raise rates again. A reading above 3.2% with firmer core prices would strengthen the case for a hike.
stories.impact: If you have a variable-rate mortgage or line of credit, or are renewing soon, this report will shape what happens to your payments in December. It will also show whether October's fuel spike reached grocery and other prices in Ontario.

stories.headline: Peltola claims victory in Alaska; race still uncalled ahead of Wednesday's ranked-choice count
stories.summary: Democrat Mary Peltola's campaign has declared victory in Alaska's U.S. Senate race, where she holds about 49.9% of first-choice votes to Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan's 46%. The Associated Press has not called the race, and a ranked-choice tabulation is set for Wednesday if no one tops 50%.
stories.now: Peltola's campaign said over the weekend that Sullivan has no mathematical path to win and that she will be elected once the remaining votes are counted. The Associated Press, which estimates about 97% of the vote is in, has not called the race, and news reports say Sullivan has not conceded or commented publicly on the count in recent days. Saturday's update from the Alaska Division of Elections added 4,290 ballots and left Peltola at 49.9% and Sullivan at 46%; Friday's count had her ahead by 10,412 votes. Overseas ballots can still arrive until Nov. 18, when a ranked-choice tabulation will redistribute the votes of trailing candidates if no one has passed 50%. An NBC News analysis says Sullivan cannot catch up through those transfers if he ends the first-choice count more than about 6,600 votes behind. A Peltola win would give Democrats 56 of 100 Senate seats. The AP has already called Alaska's governorship for Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, who takes office Dec. 7. Alaska plans to certify results on Nov. 25, and Democrats take control of both chambers of Congress in January.
stories.backstory: Republicans have held both chambers since January 2025, and all 435 House seats and about a third of the Senate were on the ballot. More than 53 million Americans voted early. Tariffs and high gas prices tied to the Iran war weighed on Trump's approval, and recent polls gave Democrats an edge in most key Senate races. Courts also turned back a Trump administration bid to set aside 20,000 California ballots.

stories.impact: Canadian exporters are watching whether a Democratic Congress moves to limit tariffs, which could ease pressure on Ontario manufacturers over time; near-term tariffs stay in place unless the White House changes them.

stories.headline: Bessent urges Nvidia to hire an outside CEO as reports say Huang is weighing a return
stories.summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Sunday that Nvidia needs a dramatic shakeup and should bring in a chief executive from outside the company, and again blamed the Commerce Department for not restricting a chip buyer linked to China. The Financial Times reported that former chief executive Jensen Huang has discussed a comeback with allies who are lobbying the board.
stories.now: Speaking on Fox News on Sunday, Bessent pressed Nvidia's board to look outside the company for its next chief executive, said scrutiny of export compliance should extend to other executives, and, according to reports, gave the board and its outside lawyers 10 days to answer whether the company pursued suspected illicit chip sales to China. Nvidia has said chief financial officer Colette Kress is interim chief executive while it considers internal and external candidates. The Financial Times reported that Huang, who resigned Wednesday, has talked with allies about returning and that they are lobbying directors. Bessent repeated that the decision on blacklisting Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based buyer of Nvidia chips, belonged to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick's department. The White House says President Trump keeps complete confidence in Lutnick, though Reuters has reported that officials have discussed whether he should go; Semafor reported Sunday that Lutnick is expected to travel with Trump to China this week. Republican Sen. Jim Banks said on Fox News Sunday that Megaspeed is still not on the export blacklist, and Senate Banking Committee chair Tim Scott has asked both Lutnick and Huang to testify; Lutnick has agreed, and reports differ on whether the Dec. 10 date is firm. CNBC reported that Nvidia is due to release quarterly results on Tuesday.
stories.backstory: Huang co-founded Nvidia and has run it since 1993, building it into the main supplier of the chips used to train artificial intelligence (AI) systems and one of the world's most valuable companies. Earlier this week, reports said the company had opened an internal investigation into whether he was targeted by a foreign intelligence effort through a relationship with a Chinese businesswoman who allegedly passed information to Beijing. Huang told staff in a company email that he had been unfaithful in his marriage. The stock had already slipped on that first report before Wednesday's news.

stories.why: Nvidia is central to the artificial intelligence (AI) boom and one of the largest stocks in major U.S. indexes, and it has never had another chief executive. The spying allegation also raises national-security questions in Washington, which controls what chips the company may sell to China.
stories.impact: Most Canadian pension plans, index funds and RRSP or TFSA portfolios that track U.S. stocks hold Nvidia, so its swings show up in retirement savings here. Quarterly results expected Tuesday and the fight over who runs the company could bring more volatility this week.

stories.headline: Zelenskyy says Tuesday's allied arms meeting must deliver as air attacks continue
stories.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Sunday night that Tuesday's meeting of Ukraine's military backers in Brussels has to produce results, above all air defence missiles. Russia and Ukraine traded air attacks again on Sunday, days after U.S.-brokered talks ended without a breakthrough.
stories.now: Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty reported that the two sides traded air attacks on Sunday, and Ukraine's General Staff said a Ukrainian strike set several storage tanks on fire at a Russian oil facility. Russia's Defence Ministry said it shot down 533 Ukrainian drones overnight, a figure that could not be independently checked, and Zelenskyy said Russian strikes hit energy facilities in the Zaporizhzhia, Sumy and Odesa regions. He said Russia launched more than 2,300 drones, 1,590 guided bombs and 15 missiles at Ukraine over the past week, and argued that many got through because of limits on Kyiv's use of SpaceX's Starshield satellite communications system. He also warned that a European security framework floated by U.S. negotiators could be used by Russia to weaken NATO. Earlier he said U.S. negotiators in Abu Dhabi asked whether Ukraine would leave the eastern Donbas region in exchange for NATO membership; Washington has not confirmed that, and U.S. envoy Jared Kushner said Saturday that the order should be a ceasefire, an end to the war and then security guarantees, with Europe's security arrangements left for after the war. Kushner says the U.S. is now trying to get Russia and European governments talking directly. European Union leaders have agreed that Britain, France, Germany, Italy and Poland, with EU officials, will speak for Europe. In his Sunday evening address, Zelenskyy said the Ukraine Defence Contact Group, the allied arms-donor forum often called the Ramstein group, must deliver results when it meets Tuesday at NATO headquarters in Brussels under British and German chairmanship; he named missiles for Patriot and NASAMS air defence systems as the priority. A separate meeting of the so-called coalition of the willing, the countries planning post-war security support for Ukraine, is planned in Berlin.
stories.backstory: U.S.-mediated efforts to end the war stalled for months while Washington focused on Iran. Rubio said in May that the effort had stagnated. Europe has repeatedly asked to be included in any deal affecting its own security.

stories.why: Linking NATO membership to land is a new idea in the talks and touches the two issues that have blocked a settlement: territory and Ukraine's long-term security. Any change to NATO's membership would need the agreement of all allies, including Canada.
stories.impact: Peace progress could ease energy and grain prices over time. Canada, a NATO and G7 member, would have a vote on any Ukrainian membership and would share in the security commitments that came with it.

stories.headline: Carney and Quebec's premier agree to talk regularly; premier defends his own U.S. outreach
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney and Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon held their first meeting on Sunday at the summit of French-speaking countries in Phnom Penh, with reports putting its length at 30 to 45 minutes. St-Pierre Plamondon, whose Parti Québécois government favours independence, called it positive but said Quebec will keep making its own case to U.S. lawmakers.
stories.now: The meeting on the sidelines of the Francophonie summit was the two leaders' first formal face-to-face talk since Quebec's Oct. 5 election, after weeks of cool relations. According to CBC, CTV and Globe and Mail reports, they agreed to work together on homelessness, to speak regularly, including on U.S. matters, and they exchanged personal phone numbers; St-Pierre Plamondon also thanked Carney for federal backing of Quebec's bid to host the Francophonie's economy ministers in 2027. Speaking to reporters afterward, the premier defended letters he sent to nearly 60 U.S. elected officials after the midterm elections, a move that had irritated Ottawa, which leads Canada's trade negotiations. Immigration, housing, the Alto high-speed rail project and a fuller discussion of U.S. trade were left for a second meeting planned in the coming weeks. The summit ends Monday. On Saturday in Manila, Canada and the Philippines closed negotiations on a free trade agreement that Carney said could help triple two-way trade to more than $10 billion a year by 2035, with signing targeted for 2027. Carney goes next to the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) leaders' meeting in Shenzhen on Nov. 18–19, where he is to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping.
stories.backstory: Canada and the Philippines first discussed a trade agreement in 2015, and Carney and Marcos agreed in October 2025 to restart and speed up the talks, alongside a separate Canada-ASEAN negotiation. The push is part of Ottawa's effort to find customers beyond the United States as tariffs from the Trump administration hit Canadian exports. The Asia trip also takes Carney to China, where he has said he will raise foreign interference with Xi; a federal public inquiry found China was the most active foreign state trying to interfere in Canadian democratic institutions. Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre has criticized the travel, saying the economy is about people struggling to make ends meet rather than summits. In Quebec, St-Pierre Plamondon leads a minority Parti Québécois government that has promised a third sovereignty referendum; reports differ on whether the target is 2029 or 2030.

stories.why: The trip is meant to show Canada can rely less on the United States for trade, and the Philippines announcement is its first concrete result, though neither agreement is signed or in force. The Cambodia stop adds a domestic test: how Ottawa and a Quebec government committed to a future sovereignty referendum will work together.
stories.impact: Nothing changes at the border yet, so prices and tariffs stay as they are until the agreement is signed and ratified, likely not before 2027. The Philippines is one of the largest sources of new immigrants to the GTA, so lower barriers could eventually matter for local importers, food businesses and Ontario exporters, including pork producers.

stories.headline: Door-to-door mail ends Monday for about 18,000 north Etobicoke homes
stories.summary: Canada Post switches about 18,000 homes in north Etobicoke from door-to-door delivery to community mailboxes on Monday, the first such change in Toronto. The rest of the GTA follows in stages through 2031.
stories.now: The change applies to homes with postal codes beginning M9V and M9W, Canada Post has confirmed. Letters and most parcels will go to a shared, locked community mailbox nearby, while oversized packages and items needing a signature will still come to the door or be held at a post office. A Rexdale letter carrier walked her last door-to-door route on Friday, according to a news report. Published schedules show Ajax, Pickering, Mississauga and Brampton switching between September and November 2027, with North York and most of downtown Toronto last, by September 2031. Canada Post says people who cannot get to a community mailbox can apply for accommodations such as a more accessible compartment or weekly home delivery; the postal workers' union and disability advocates say the change will be hard on some residents.
stories.backstory: Canada Post has lost money for years as letter volumes fall and parcel competition grows. In September 2025 the federal government lifted its freeze on community mailbox conversions and told the Crown corporation to move the roughly four million addresses that still get door-to-door delivery. Canada Post said in April 2026 that the national switch should take about five years. An earlier conversion program that began in 2014 was halted after public opposition and formally cancelled in 2018. Sept-Îles, Que., and Winnipeg were the first to switch under the new plan in October, with Etobicoke and the Moncton, N.B., area following in November.

timeline.event: Ottawa lifts freeze on community mailbox conversions

stories.why: This is the first Toronto neighbourhood to lose home delivery under a plan that will eventually reach every GTA address that still has it. Canada Post says serving a door costs about twice as much as serving a community mailbox.
stories.impact: If your postal code starts with M9V or M9W, your mail goes to a community mailbox from Monday; check the notice Canada Post sent for your mailbox location and keys. Elsewhere in the GTA nothing changes yet, but you can check your area's date on Canada Post's website and apply for an accommodation if mobility is an issue.

stories.headline: Van Hollen claims 'about 15' backers in Senate leader race; Schumer still favoured
stories.summary: Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen told Fox News Sunday that about 15 senators support his bid to replace Chuck Schumer as Senate Democratic leader and that the number is growing. Schumer says he has the votes for the Dec. 1 secret ballot and remains the clear favourite.
stories.now: On Fox News Sunday, Van Hollen put his support at about 15 senators and growing, dismissed reports that he cannot win and called the race very open. On CNN's State of the Union he said several senators on a list of Schumer supporters released by Schumer's side have privately promised to vote for him instead, without naming them, and on ABC's This Week he accused Schumer's team of spreading misinformation and trying to instill fear. His public backers include Sens. Bernie Sanders and Jeff Merkley and Senators-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan and Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota. Schumer said after the election that he has the votes, and his allies have predicted more than 40; Democrats will hold 55 or 56 seats depending on Alaska, so the winner needs 28 or 29. Published tallies of public endorsements still show Schumer well ahead, with a New Republic count listing 16 lawmakers for him. The ballot is secret, so neither side's claims can be checked before the vote.
stories.backstory: Schumer, of New York, has led Senate Democrats since 2017, as majority leader from 2021 to 2025 and minority leader since. Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress in the Nov. 3 midterms and take over in January. Schumer faced criticism within his party during the campaign, and Van Hollen broke with party leadership by endorsing El-Sayed in Michigan's Democratic primary in June. Whoever leads the majority decides which bills and nominees reach the Senate floor.

stories.why: The majority leader controls the Senate's agenda, including whether and when votes on tariffs, spending and oversight of the White House happen. The contest is the first test of unity for Democrats since their midterm win.
stories.impact: There is no direct effect on Ontario for now. The winner will shape how hard the Senate pushes back on tariffs against Canada when the new Congress sits in January.

stories.headline: Eisenkot's and Netanyahu's parties open coalition talks; Israeli media report no progress
stories.summary: Negotiators for Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party and Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud met Sunday to discuss a possible unity government in Israel and agreed only to keep talking. The two men each insist on being prime minister.
stories.now: Likud was represented by Knesset member Ofir Katz and Michael Rabello, a former personal lawyer to Netanyahu, and Yashar by Knesset member Chili Tropper and Yoav Horowitz. Both sides described the meeting as businesslike and said dialogue will continue. Yashar denied an Army Radio report that it had offered to rotate the premiership, saying its only proposal is for Likud to join a government led by Eisenkot; Netanyahu has said he should lead any unity government and wants his current allies included. Israel's Channel 12 reported that the session produced no progress, and the head of the ultra-Orthodox United Torah Judaism party denied reports of significant progress in its own contacts with Eisenkot's bloc. The next test is a parliamentary vote expected Tuesday on making Yashar's Matan Kahana speaker of the Knesset. Eisenkot, who called off an earlier round on Nov. 10 over a speech Netanyahu gave in parliament, has until Dec. 6 to assemble a majority, and the president can extend that by up to 14 days. Separately, an Israeli strike on Saturday in southern Gaza killed Samir Abu Younis, commander of Hamas's Rafah brigade, which both Hamas and Israel's military confirmed despite the ceasefire in place since October 2025.
stories.backstory: Israel voted on Oct. 27 and neither Netanyahu's right-wing and religious bloc nor the opposition bloc led by Eisenkot, a former army chief, won 61 of the 120 seats in the Knesset (parliament). President Isaac Herzog gave Eisenkot the first try at forming a government on Nov. 7 after parties holding 67 seats recommended him, against 46 for Netanyahu. Eisenkot has said he will not serve under Netanyahu, who remains caretaker prime minister. If no one can form a government, Israel faces another election.

stories.why: Who leads Israel affects the course of the war with Iran, the Gaza ceasefire and relations with Washington. The coalition arithmetic remains difficult for both men.
stories.impact: Effects on Ontario are indirect: regional stability feeds into oil and gasoline prices, and Toronto's large Jewish, Israeli and Palestinian communities follow these events closely.

stories.headline: Former Kitchener MP Mike Morrice wins Green Party leadership with 96.6% of the vote
stories.summary: The Green Party of Canada announced Saturday that Mike Morrice, the only candidate on the ballot, is its new leader. He succeeds Elizabeth May, who remains the party's only member of Parliament.
stories.now: Morrice received 96.6% of the vote, the party said; members could either vote for him or choose none of the above, and Radio-Canada reported that 3,435 votes were counted. He became the only candidate in September when Nira Dookeran withdrew for personal and family reasons, but party rules still required a vote. May welcomed the result warmly. Morrice does not hold a seat in the House of Commons, so May continues as the Greens' sole voice there.
stories.backstory: Morrice, the founder of an environmental non-profit, won Kitchener Centre for the Greens in 2021, the party's first federal seat in Ontario, and served as its critic for housing and disability inclusion. He lost the riding in the April 2025 federal election to Conservative Kelly DeRidder by fewer than 400 votes. May said after that election that she would step down as leader, a job she has held for most of the past two decades. Morrice was named deputy leader in November 2025 and left that post to run.

timeline.event: Morrice narrowly loses Kitchener Centre; May later says she will step down as leader
Morrice named deputy leader

stories.why: The Greens hold one seat in a Parliament where Prime Minister Mark Carney's Liberals govern without a large cushion, and a new leader from Ontario changes where the party is likely to focus. Morrice will have to rebuild a party that lost ground in 2025 while leading it from outside the Commons.
stories.impact: Nothing changes immediately for Ontario residents. Kitchener Centre and nearby Waterloo Region ridings are the likeliest places to see a stronger Green campaign in the next federal election, which could affect close three-way races there.

stories.headline: Three children and two adults critically hurt in Burlington townhouse fire
stories.summary: Five people, including three children, are in life-threatening condition after a fire in a Burlington townhouse early Saturday. Ontario's Fire Marshal is investigating and no cause has been given.
stories.now: Halton police said the fire broke out shortly before 7 a.m. at a townhouse complex at 1300 Maple Crossing Blvd., near Freeman Street. Burlington firefighters pulled the occupants out and put the fire out before it spread to neighbouring units. Two adults and three children were taken to hospital with life-threatening injuries; CBC reported that three of the patients had no vital signs when first reached and are now listed as critical, and paramedics said a sixth person had lesser injuries. Local reports citing police say one child is about 12 and the other two are believed to be five or younger, that the fire began in a bedroom, and that damage is estimated at $350,000. No update on the victims' conditions had been released by Sunday evening. Fire Chief Drew Boys said the investigation is at an early stage and that nothing has been ruled out, including whether the fire was suspicious and whether smoke alarms were working.
stories.backstory: The fire was in a multi-unit townhouse complex in central Burlington, a city of about 190,000 people in Halton Region west of Toronto. In Ontario, the Office of the Fire Marshal investigates fires that cause deaths or serious injuries, working alongside local police and fire services. Those investigations look at where a fire started, what caused it and whether smoke alarms were installed and working. Ontario law requires a working smoke alarm on every storey of a home and outside all sleeping areas.

timeline.event: Fire reported at Maple Crossing Blvd. townhouse shortly before 7 a.m.

stories.why: Five people from one home, three of them children, are fighting for their lives, and investigators have not yet said how the fire started. The findings on cause and on smoke alarms could matter for fire-safety enforcement in similar housing.
stories.impact: There is no continuing danger to neighbours, but expect police and fire crews around Maple Crossing Boulevard while the investigation continues. It is a reminder to test smoke alarms on every floor and to make sure everyone at home knows two ways out.
